cards.front: In developing neural circuits, a {{c1::target}} is the tissue an axon grows to and connects with.
cards.back: Examples include a limb muscle or a gland.
cards.quote: A target is the tissue an axon grows to and connects with

cards.front: A cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord is a {{c1::ganglion}}.
cards.quote: A ganglion is a cluster of neuron cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord

cards.front: After an embryonic limb is removed, the associated sensory ganglion is small at the final count. What measurements would distinguish reduced neuron production from later loss?
cards.back: Count neurons at several developmental stages and mark dividing and dying cells. Low production supports fewer births; normal early counts followed by increased death support later loss.
cards.quote: You need counts at a series of stages, with dividing and dying cells marked.

cards.front: Which developing neuron populations are covered by the NGF survival rule?
cards.back: Sympathetic neurons and TrkA-bearing sensory neurons, mostly small pain- and temperature-sensing neurons, during their windows of dependence.
cards.quote: sympathetic neurons, and the sensory neurons that carry TrkA, the receptor NGF binds

cards.front: How does the neurotrophic hypothesis link a target to the number of developing neurons that survive?
cards.back: Targets supply a limiting survival factor that reaching axons take up. Neurons compete for it; those obtaining too little undergo apoptosis.
cards.quote: neurons compete for a limiting amount of neurotrophic factor, which their targets supply
cards.section: The hypothesis and what it predicts

cards.front: A developing neuron population depends on a limiting resource supplied by its target. Predict the effects of reducing versus enlarging that target, and explain why.
cards.back: Reducing the target should increase death; enlarging it should reduce death. Changing target support changes how many already-produced neurons can survive.
cards.quote: Remove the target, and more neurons die.
cards.section: The hypothesis and what it predicts

cards.front: According to the neurotrophic hypothesis, when should most target-dependent neuronal death occur?
cards.back: Around the time axons reach their targets and begin to compete.
cards.quote: Most of the death should happen around the time axons reach the target and begin to compete.
cards.section: The hypothesis and what it predicts

cards.front: Chick embryos with an extra leg had unchanged early lumbar motor neuron counts but more neurons later when the graft moved vigorously. What does this support, and what remains unidentified?
cards.back: Extra target reduces neuron death rather than increasing early production. The limiting resource is unidentified; these motor neurons do not depend on NGF.
cards.quote: The result supports a limiting target resource but says nothing about which molecule
cards.section: The hypothesis and what it predicts

cards.front: A factor that is enough by itself to produce a specified effect is {{c1::sufficient}} for that effect.
cards.quote: A factor is sufficient if it is enough, by itself, to produce an effect.

cards.front: A factor without which a specified effect does not occur is {{c1::necessary}} for that effect.
cards.quote: It is necessary if the effect does not happen without it.

cards.front: Purified NGF injection enlarges sympathetic ganglia in young mammals. What does this establish before neuron production and death have been measured?
cards.back: NGF is sufficient to enlarge ganglia. Enlargement alone does not establish whether neurons were saved, newly produced, or simply grew larger.
cards.quote: A larger ganglion does not yet say whether neurons were saved or born.

cards.front: What happened to sympathetic ganglia when newborn mice received NGF-neutralizing antiserum?
cards.back: The sympathetic ganglia were destroyed.
cards.quote: Levi-Montalcini and Booker injected it into newborn mice, with rats and other mammals for comparison. The sympathetic ganglia were destroyed.

cards.front: Why does the weaker effect of NGF antiserum in older animals matter for interpreting NGF dependence?
cards.back: Dependence is tied to a developmental window that differs between populations. A weak effect later does not exclude a strong earlier survival requirement.
cards.quote: dependence on NGF is tied to a developmental window, and the window differs between populations.

cards.front: An animal whose gene is disrupted so that it makes no working protein is a {{c1::knockout}} for that gene.
cards.quote: A knockout mouse has a gene disrupted so that it makes no working protein
cards.section: Delete it, and watch the time course

cards.front: Neutralizing factor X causes developing neurons to disappear, but the antibody might bind another protein. What independent perturbation would directly test that concern?
cards.back: Delete the gene for X and ask whether the same neurons are lost. This removes X without exposing neurons to the potentially cross-reactive antibody.
cards.quote: A knockout mouse has a gene disrupted so that it makes no working protein, and it settles the antibody doubt.
cards.section: Delete it, and watch the time course

cards.front: Mouse TrkA-null superior cervical ganglia have normal early neuron counts and neurogenesis, followed by a growing deficit and more dying nuclei. Which developmental process failed?
cards.back: Survival failed after the neurons were produced, rather than neurogenesis.
cards.quote: the shortfall came from more dying cells, not fewer dividing ones.
cards.section: Delete it, and watch the time course

cards.front: How does NGF support mouse sympathetic neuron survival in relation to Bax?
cards.back: NGF holds back a Bax-dependent death program; neurons lacking Bax can survive NGF withdrawal.
cards.quote: So NGF works by holding back a Bax-dependent death program.
cards.section: Delete it, and watch the time course

cards.front: Two cultures of mouse sympathetic neurons receive NGF. One lacks Bax; the other does not. After NGF withdrawal, which should retain more live neurons, and why?
cards.back: The Bax-null culture should retain more. Withdrawal-induced death requires Bax, so deleting Bax prevents the death program that NGF normally restrains.
cards.quote: in culture, sympathetic neurons lacking Bax survive when NGF is withdrawn.
cards.section: Delete it, and watch the time course

cards.front: Extra NGF is supplied only during the normal death window of an NGF-dependent sensory ganglion. With production unchanged, what happens to neuron number and identity, and why?
cards.back: More existing neurons should survive, retaining their specified identity. Survival support reduces normal loss; it does not itself specify a new neuronal type.
cards.quote: Given during the death period, NGF enlarges the ganglia mainly because more of the neurons that were made escape the normal death.

cards.front: During a defined death window, extra factor X yields more neurons, fewer dying nuclei, unchanged cumulative production and stable lineage. Does this establish sufficiency, necessity, or both for survival support?
cards.back: Sufficiency for increased survival in this setting. The survival checks distinguish rescue from extra production or fate change; necessity still requires removing X and testing survival.
cards.quote: If NGF acts on survival, the counts match early and diverge only during the death period, and the treated ganglia contain fewer pyknotic nuclei.

cards.front: Why can a short pulse of a DNA-copying marker fail to show whether total neuron production changed?
cards.back: It measures precursors copying DNA at that moment, not cumulative neuron production. Combine cell-cycle measurements with birthdating or lineage tracing across the interval.
cards.quote: shows how many precursors are copying DNA, not how many neurons are produced.

cards.front: After factor treatment, more cells carry the expected neuronal markers. How would you test whether they are surviving members of the original cohort rather than cells converted to that identity?
cards.back: Label the original cohort by lineage tracing or pulse-chase birthdating and follow its survival. The rule is that identity markers alone cannot exclude fate conversion.
cards.quote: Markers alone cannot exclude a fate change, because converted cells would carry the same markers in the same place.

cards.front: Why must early NGF treatment in chick primary sympathetic ganglia be assessed separately from NGF treatment during the main death period?
cards.back: Very early NGF can increase precursor division as well as reduce death. A larger ganglion then need not reflect survival alone.
cards.quote: Very early, before sympathetic axons reach their targets, extra NGF can also increase division in the primary sympathetic ganglia

cards.front: In the ideal survival model, N neurons have already been made, supply is F units/day, and each survivor needs at least q units/day: S ≤ {{c1::min(N, floor(F/q))}}.
cards.back: The bound assumes no neurons are added.
cards.quote: S survivors take at least S × q, which cannot exceed F

cards.front: Why can a factor acting only on survival never leave more neurons alive than were originally made?
cards.back: It can prevent loss of existing neurons but cannot produce additional neurons. Once every neuron is supported, more factor adds no survivors.
cards.quote: Once every neuron that was made is supported, more factor adds no survivors.

cards.front: In a hypothetical ideal survival model, 1,200 neurons are already made. Supply is 900 units/day and each survivor needs 2 units/day. What is the maximum supported count, and what limits it?
cards.back: Supply capacity = floor(900 units/day ÷ 2 units/neuron/day) = 450 neurons. The upper bound is min(1,200, 450) = 450 neurons; supply limits it.
cards.quote: S survivors take at least S × q, which cannot exceed F

cards.front: A hypothetical fixed cohort starts with 2,000 neurons. Untreated, 1,200 survive; with a survival factor, 1,800 survive. Production is unchanged. What percentage of normally dying neurons was saved?
cards.back: Normally lost = 2,000 − 1,200 = 800 neurons. Saved = 1,800 − 1,200 = 600. Fraction saved = 600/800 = 0.75, or 75%.
cards.quote: the larger ganglia are made of neurons that would have died, and their number stays at or below the number made.

cards.front: In the ideal survival model, every member of a fixed neuron cohort already receives enough factor. What happens to the survivor ceiling if factor supply doubles, and why?
cards.back: The ceiling stays at the cohort size. Supply is already sufficient, so the number made remains the limiting bound.
cards.quote: Extra factor raises the second term. Acting as a survival factor, nothing raises the first.

cards.front: Why can a developing ganglion remain below the number of neurons originally made even with abundant survival factor?
cards.back: Some neurons die for reasons that the factor cannot fix. An upper bound does not guarantee that every neuron survives.
cards.quote: Some die for reasons NGF cannot fix, so even plenty of NGF can leave the count below the number made.

cards.front: A fixed neuron cohort shares a limited survival supply equally, leaving every cell below its minimum requirement. Does the ideal capacity bound guarantee that some reach survival, and why?
cards.back: No; even none may survive. If many cells commit to death before supply is redistributed, the remaining capacity cannot rescue them. The bound is a maximum, not a prediction.
cards.quote: If many commit before it is shared out again, far fewer are left, perhaps none.
cards.section: A puzzle hidden in the ceiling

cards.front: How can an initial NGF advantage amplify itself in the mouse sympathetic-neuron competition model?
cards.back: NGF raises the level of its own receptor, TrkA. A neuron receiving slightly more NGF can then take up still more.
cards.quote: NGF raises the level of its own receptor, TrkA, in the neurons that receive it
cards.section: A puzzle hidden in the ceiling

cards.front: In the mouse sympathetic-neuron competition model, through which receptor do winners’ BDNF and NT-4 promote death in weakly NGF-signalling neighbours?
cards.quote: These act through a second receptor, p75, on neighbours whose NGF signalling is weak, and push them toward death
cards.section: A puzzle hidden in the ceiling

cards.front: A dose of NGF rescues developing sympathetic neurons. Predict its effect on normal chick limb motor neuron death, and explain the population limit.
cards.back: Limb motor neuron death should remain roughly unchanged. Those neurons do not depend on NGF; a survival result transfers only to the relevant population and its factor.
cards.quote: in chick embryos several other factors each reduce part of their normal death, and extra NGF should leave it roughly unchanged.
cards.section: A puzzle hidden in the ceiling

cards.front: A signal that allows an outcome chosen by something else is {{c1::permissive}}.
cards.quote: A permissive signal allows an outcome that something else chooses.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: A signal that chooses the outcome itself is {{c1::instructive}}.
cards.quote: An instructive signal chooses the outcome itself.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: A developmental factor is needed for cells to survive, and restoring its normal distribution restores a spatial pattern. How would you test whether it also specifies that pattern?
cards.back: Keep survival supported while supplying the factor uniformly or at a new location. A pattern following delivery supports instruction; a persisting normal pattern supports permission. Necessity alone cannot distinguish them.
cards.quote: What separates them is changing where or when the signal is delivered while keeping it present.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: NGF is produced selectively in mouse pancreatic islets. Sympathetic innervation rises there without a matching rise nearby. What does the spatial selectivity support?
cards.back: NGF is instructive for local innervation in this setting: the pattern follows the altered source. This does not establish the same role in every target.
cards.quote: Sympathetic innervation of the islets rose sharply, with no matching rise in the tissue around them.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: Mouse sympathetic neurons make their own NGF: axons reach targets but branch sparsely within them. Local islet NGF restores islet innervation. What distinction does this support?
cards.back: In the targets examined, the results fit a model in which NGF is permissive for reaching a target and instructive for branching density and location within it. Altering the source does not prove all guidance gradients were absent.
cards.quote: NGF is permissive for reaching a target and instructive for how densely, and where, axons innervate within it.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: Sympathetic neurons survive in mice lacking both NGF and Bax but fail to innervate many targets. What does blocking death allow this experiment to establish?
cards.back: NGF has functions beyond survival. The rule is that Bax deletion removes death as the explanation for the remaining innervation defects.
cards.quote: In mice lacking both NGF and Bax, sympathetic neurons survive without NGF, so any remaining defect is not about survival.
cards.section: Permissive for survival, instructive for wiring

cards.front: Suppose normal death is rare in a defined enteric neuron population. Adding factor X leaves its number unchanged. Does that rule out a survival requirement for X, and what test follows?
cards.back: No. Existing support may already suffice, leaving no loss to rescue. By the ceiling rule, extra support need not raise counts; remove X during defined intervals to test necessity.
cards.quote: If normal death is rare, adding X may not raise survival because endogenous support already suffices

cards.front: A target makes and releases factor X. What targeted deletion and rescue experiment would strengthen the claim that target-derived X supports neurons, while avoiding destruction of the target itself?
cards.back: Delete X only in the intact target, measure neuronal death, and test rescue with local X. The rule is that target removal changes many things; a source-specific loss and rescue isolate X more closely.
cards.quote: Delete X only in that tissue, leaving the tissue intact, and check that the neurons die and that local X rescues them.

cards.front: Why does an NGF response in cultured basal forebrain cholinergic neurons not establish that NGF is required for their development?
cards.back: These neurons still develop in NGF-null mice. Ability to respond to a factor does not establish a requirement for it.
cards.quote: Basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, which respond to NGF in culture, still develop in NGF-null mice.

cards.front: How can a survival factor supplied by a distant target support a neuron’s cell body?
cards.back: It acts at the axon ending, and a signal returns to the cell body to support survival.
cards.quote: The factor acts at the axon ending, and a signal returns to the cell body to support survival.
cards.section: How a distant target reaches the cell body

cards.front: Why should complete target innervation not be used as an absolute prerequisite for neurotrophin dependence in the mouse superior cervical ganglion?
cards.back: Some neurons may become dependent a little before target innervation is complete.
cards.quote: some neurons may come to depend on neurotrophins a little before target innervation is complete.
cards.section: When the superior cervical ganglion starts to depend

cards.front: In embryos from Toll-mutant fly mothers, injected wild-type cytoplasm restores a ventralmost region wherever it is injected. Does delivery supply permissive or instructive information, and why?
cards.back: Instructive information: the rescued pattern follows the arbitrary injection site, rather than merely reappearing at a fixed location.
cards.quote: the ventralmost part of the rescued pattern formed at the injection site, wherever the needle went in.
cards.section: A fly example of permissive versus instructive
